issues.legal_issue: A letters patent appeal is maintainable when a petition invoking both constitutional supervisory jurisdictions is, in substance, decided under the jurisdiction that permits such an appeal.
material_facts: The landlord’s petition invoked both constitutional jurisdictions and sought to quash the decisions of the rent authorities.
The single judge examined the merits, set aside the rent authorities’ decisions, and did not state that the order was made under the supervisory jurisdiction.
The tenants appealed to the division bench, which dismissed the appeal as not maintainable.
issues.conclusion: The petition and the single judge’s order were in substance under Article 226, so the letters patent appeal was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Under Umaji Keshao Meshram v. Smt. Radhikabai, where the facts justify a petition under either Article 226 or Article 227 and the petitioner invokes both, the court should treat it as under Article 226 to preserve the appeal right; ancillary directions concerning Article 227 do not defeat that right when the substantial part of the order is under Article 226. The Court held that the contrary use of Umaji by the Full Bench in Sushilabai Laxminarayan Mudliyar v. Nihalchand Waghajibhai Shaha was incorrect.

predicates.appeal_from_single_judge_order: A party appealed from an order made by a single judge.
predicates.petition_invokes_both_jurisdictions: The underlying petition invoked both constitutional jurisdictions and the facts supported seeking relief under either.
predicates.merits_review_under_appellate_jurisdicti: The single judge substantially reviewed the merits and set aside the decisions under challenge, without stating that the order was made only in supervisory jurisdiction.

issues.definition: When a party appeals a single judge’s merits decision on a petition invoking both jurisdictions, and the decision substantially exercises the jurisdiction that permits an appeal, the letters patent appeal is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant is not habitually in arrears merely because rent was paid at irregular intervals when the landlord had long accepted that practice without objection and the tenant had no arrears when eviction proceedings began.
material_facts: For years, the landlord’s agent collected rent at his convenience, and the parties followed a practice of paying rent in lump sums rather than month by month.
The landlord accepted delayed payments without objection, and rent was also sometimes paid in advance.
The tenants said there was no alternative arrangement for paying rent and replied to the landlord’s first demand for monthly payment by disputing default.
No rent was in arrears when the landlord filed the eviction application, and the landlord did not establish that rent had gone unpaid when his agent came to collect it.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were not habitual defaulters; the single judge’s finding of habitual default was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Clause 13(3)(ii) of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949 requires proof that the tenant was habitually in arrears. Habitual delay does not include bona fide payment in response to the landlord’s demand or payment when the landlord’s agent comes to collect rent, where the landlord has long accepted the practice without objection. Applying Rashik Lal v. Shah Gokuldas, a landlord who accepts delayed rent without objection cannot suddenly seek eviction without first warning the tenant that regular payment will be required.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding_for_hab: The landlord sought eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground that the tenant was habitually in arrears.
predicates.landlord_long_accepted_irregular_payment: The landlord repeatedly accepted rent paid at irregular intervals without objecting to the timing.
predicates.tenant_paid_bona_fide_under_collection_p: The tenant paid rent in good faith under a longstanding practice in which the landlord or the landlord’s agent collected it.
predicates.no_arrears_when_proceeding_filed: No rent was outstanding when the landlord began the eviction proceeding.

issues.definition: In a rent-control eviction proceeding based on habitual arrears, a tenant who paid in good faith under a collection practice long accepted without objection and had no arrears when the proceeding began is not habitually in arrears.

issues.legal_issue: A finding of bona fide need may be maintained while the extent of that need and a related reconstruction claim are remanded for determination after the parties have an opportunity to amend their pleadings and present evidence.
material_facts: The landlord established that the premises came to him in a partition, and the tenants had paid rent to him for many years.

The single judge found the landlord’s evidence of bona fide need sufficient and found that the rent authorities had wrongly rejected it, including on the basis that some witnesses were related or interested.

The single judge remanded the matter to determine the extent of the landlord’s need for residence and a clinic or dispensary, and to examine the reconstruction claim, with an opportunity for amended pleadings and evidence.
issues.conclusion: The finding of bona fide need and the remand for determining its extent and considering reconstruction were maintained.
issues.legal_principle: Under clauses 13(3)(vi) and 13(3)(vii) of the C.P. and Berar Letting of Houses and Rent Control Order, 1949, the Court upheld the bona fide-need finding and the direction to determine the extent of need and examine reconstruction after giving the parties a full opportunity to amend pleadings and lead evidence. The judgment identifies no earlier case relied on for this issue.

predicates.rent_control_eviction_proceeding_for_bon: The landlord sought eviction in a rent-control proceeding on the ground of bona fide need.
predicates.landlord_established_ownership_and_need_: The landlord established a basis for ownership of the premises and presented evidence supporting the asserted need.
predicates.extent_of_need_or_reconstruction_unresol: The extent of the landlord’s need or a related reconstruction claim remained to be determined.
predicates.parties_need_opportunity_to_amend_and_pr: The parties required an opportunity to amend their pleadings and present evidence on the unresolved matters.

issues.definition: When a landlord establishes evidence supporting bona fide need but its extent or a related reconstruction claim remains unresolved, the finding may be maintained while those matters are remanded for further pleadings and evidence.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may hear the merits itself rather than remand a maintainable appeal when the litigation has already been prolonged and the underlying matter has already been remanded.
material_facts: The litigation had continued for nearly a decade.
The single judge had already remanded the matter to the rent controller.
After concluding that the letters patent appeal was maintainable, the Supreme Court heard the tenants’ appeal on the merits rather than sending it back to the division bench.
issues.conclusion: In the interest of justice, the Supreme Court heard and decided the appeal on the merits instead of remanding it to the division bench.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered it proper, in the interest of justice, to decide the merits itself in view of the length of the litigation and the existing remand. The judgment states no earlier case or statutory provision as the basis for this procedural choice.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_appellate_disposition: A party appealed from an appellate court’s disposition of a matter.
predicates.litigation_prolonged: The litigation had already continued for a substantial time.
predicates.underlying_matter_already_remanded: The underlying matter had already been remanded for further proceedings.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows prolonged litigation and the underlying matter has already been remanded, the appellate court may decide the merits itself rather than remand the appeal for another decision.
